 The open enrollment question: Will home health be there after discharge? 
 Julie Smith 
 November 18, 2026 
 Share › 
 Share on Facebook 
 Share on Twitter 
 Share on LinkedIn 
 Share by Email 
 Print 
 Every fall, Medicare beneficiaries shop for private Medicare plans by comparing premiums, prescription drug coverage, provider networks and extra benefits. Those are important aspects, no doubt, but there is another area of a Medicare Advantage (MA) plan that few people consider: If I leave the hospital needing home healthcare, how quickly will someone arrive? Will someone arrive at all?
 For many patients, no one arrives. According to research from CareJourney , only 61% of Medicare beneficiaries referred to home health after a hospitalization received services within seven days of discharge. More than 1 in 3 went home without receiving that care during the first week. Access was even worse for patients eligible for both Medicare and Medicaid, with just 53% receiving services.
 A referral on a hospital discharge summary is no guarantee that a nurse or therapist will show up. Patients need and deserve better options because the consequences can be serious.
 When a referral does not become care
 In CareJourney’s analysis, patients who went home without home health during the first week had a 40% readmission rate over 90 days, compared with 30% among those who received care. Average 90-day spending was about $2,500 higher. These are signs that a missed visit leads to worse care.
 A patient recovering from heart failure may need medication checks and monitoring. Someone who has lost mobility may need therapy before a fall sends them back to the hospital. Family caregivers cannot fill every clinical gap.
 Hospital discharge teams and home health agencies see the other side of the problem. An agency listed in a plan directory may have no nurse available for that patient or their clinical needs. A referral can be sent several times before anyone accepts it. The hospital needs a safe discharge, the agency needs usable clinical information, and the health plan needs to know whether the patient received care. Without someone managing the handoff, each organization may assume another has taken care of it.
 A different way to manage home health
 A different approach gives home health agencies responsibility for seeing the referral through. Under delegated arrangements with MA plans, tango takes financial responsibility for home health services and manages the steps from referral to placement. Teams track patients approaching discharge, identify agencies that can take them, and stay involved when a referral stalls. The agency has a consistent partner for payment and clinical questions, and the plan can see whether its member started care.
 This approach has proven results. In one large regional health plan tango works with, the average time to start home health was 0.9 days, against a 3.5-day contractual target. We regularly achieve a 100% placement rate for members transitioning from hospital to home care. Across tango-managed markets, 98% of qualified referrals start care within 48 hours.
 Our analyses also show unplanned readmissions 35% below benchmarks, while member satisfaction across our business is 97–98%. These are company-reported results across different populations, but they illustrate measures plans and patients should expect: accepted referrals, timely visits, fewer readmissions and a positive care experience.
 Why the incentives need to change
 Why is this still uncommon? Home health agencies have limited staff and must choose which patients they can serve. MA plans that focus on lowering per-visit payments or use prior authorization controls can make difficult placements that much less attractive. A network may look extensive on paper without having capacity when it counts.
 Complex medical cases can be harder to place than predictable surgical discharges. CareJourney found that only 56% of patients referred after medical hospitalizations received home health in the first week, compared with 75% of surgical referrals.
 Payment design helps explain why tango’s business model can work. Prospective payments for an episode of care give agencies flexibility to provide the visits a patient needs. Bonuses timely starts recognize the work of accepting referrals. Shared savings tied to fewer readmissions reward performance. When plans and agencies have reason to care about the full recovery, they are less likely to treat the referral as a completed transaction before a clinician arrives.
 Open enrollment gives beneficiaries a chance to compare what plans promise, but little information about whether a plan can deliver home health after discharge. Most people don’t know how a plan finds an available agency or what happens when a referral is declined, and they shouldn’t have to. After a hospitalization, patients and their families have enough to manage without worrying whether the care prescribed for them will arrive.
 That’s where tango comes in. We manage the transition from hospital to home so that referrals translate into timely care, better outcomes and a smoother recovery. For patients and their families, that means greater confidence that the care they need will be there when they need it.
 Julie Smith is chief growth officer of tango .
